subtopic_detail: sequencing specialist referral and concurrent mood treatment for a young person seeking gender related care
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17 year old patient who was assigned female at birth, identifies as male and uses he and him. He has lived as male at school and at home for two years with his family's support and has not previously been referred to any specialist service.

He describes five months of low mood, loss of interest in soccer which he used to play weekly, and broken sleep. He links the distress to chest development and to being repeatedly misnamed by a group at school. He has no plan or intent to harm himself and has never self harmed. He is attending school, has close friends, and is not using alcohol or other drugs. He asks you what medical options exist and says he wants to know what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows reactive but low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, iron studies within normal limits, no current medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence testosterone therapy in the general practice at today's visit
options.rationale: Gender affirming hormone therapy in a person under 18 follows assessment by an experienced multidisciplinary team, with consideration of fertility preservation and the relevant consent framework. Initiating it at a first general practice visit bypasses each of those steps. (Source: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health)
source_refs: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health

options.text: Treat the depression first and defer the gender discussion until it lifts
options.rationale: Sequencing care this way is intuitive because clinicians reasonably want a clear assessment, but the distress here is substantially driven by the very issues being deferred, so the depression is unlikely to lift while they remain unaddressed. Deferral is itself experienced as a barrier and is associated with disengagement from care. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary gender service and treat the low mood now
options.rationale: Assessment for gender related medical care in a person under 18 is undertaken by a multidisciplinary service, and referral should not wait for mental health difficulties to resolve because the distress is closely tied to the unresolved gender related concerns and to the bullying. Treating the depressive symptoms concurrently with psychological therapy and school advocacy addresses both strands at once. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Advise that no step can be considered until he turns eighteen years old
options.rationale: Australian practice provides for assessment and, where appropriate, treatment of people under 18 through specialist services, and turning 18 is not a legal or clinical threshold for beginning assessment. A blanket deferral leaves the current distress untreated. (Source: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health)
source_refs: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health

options.text: Refer for therapy aimed at exploring whether this identity will persist
options.rationale: Therapy directed at changing or discouraging a person's gender identity is ineffective, is associated with worse mental health outcomes, and is prohibited by legislation in several Australian jurisdictions. Exploratory psychological support is part of specialist assessment, but it is not framed as testing whether the identity is genuine. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Trans and gender diverse young people have substantially higher rates of depression, anxiety, self harm and suicidal ideation than their peers, and the evidence indicates that this excess is driven predominantly by external factors including bullying, family rejection, misgendering and barriers to care rather than by gender identity itself. Family support and the ability to use one's name and pronouns are among the strongest protective factors identified. The Australian standards of care set out a multidisciplinary model in which assessment covers gender identity and its development, mental health, family and social circumstances, and fertility considerations, and in which psychological support, social affirmation, medical options and advocacy in school settings all sit within the same plan. Mental health treatment proceeds in parallel rather than as a prerequisite, because delaying access while waiting for symptoms to remit both prolongs distress and is associated with disengagement. Practices aimed at changing or suppressing gender identity are ineffective, are linked to worse outcomes and are unlawful in several Australian jurisdictions.
key_points: Excess mental illness in this group is driven largely by external stressors, not identity
Family support and correct name and pronoun use are strong protective factors
Assessment for those under 18 is multidisciplinary and includes fertility discussion
Treat mental health concerns in parallel rather than as a prerequisite to referral
Practices aimed at changing gender identity are ineffective and unlawful in several jurisdictions
explanation.pearls: Consistent use of a young person's chosen name across home, school and health settings is associated with a substantial reduction in depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation, which makes documenting the name and pronouns in the medical record a clinical intervention rather than an administrative one.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents
Australian Professional Association for Trans Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: managing an elevated mood syndrome emerging on high dose corticosteroid when the steroid must continue
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 58 year old man on the respiratory ward. He was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily eleven days ago for a severe exacerbation of an inflammatory lung condition and the respiratory team say he needs to remain on a substantial dose for now.

Over the past four days the nursing staff report he has slept about two hours a night, has been talking rapidly and constantly to other patients, and yesterday telephoned a real estate agent about buying an investment property he cannot afford. He tells you he has never felt sharper and that he has worked out how to fix the hospital's discharge system. He has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness and his urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Examination: Elevated and expansive mood, pressured speech with flight of ideas, grandiose plans without fixed delusional conviction, no perceptual disturbance, orientated to time place and person, attention intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, sodium within normal limits, glucose 11.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), C reactive protein falling, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in a week
options.rationale: Corticosteroids can produce depressive as well as elevated states, and an antidepressant would be considered for the former. Giving one during an elevated episode risks worsening it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the corticosteroid abruptly today and observe him on the ward
options.rationale: Stopping abruptly after eleven days of high dose therapy risks adrenal insufficiency and would allow the lung disease to flare, which is a worse outcome than the psychiatric syndrome being treated. Corticosteroids are reduced in a planned way, not stopped outright. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate with monitoring of the serum lithium level
options.rationale: Lithium has been used prophylactically in patients requiring repeated corticosteroid courses, which gives this option some basis, but it has a slow onset, a narrow therapeutic index and requires stable fluid balance and renal function in an acutely unwell inpatient. It is not the treatment for an episode that is already established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss dose reduction with the treating team and commence olanzapine
options.rationale: The disturbance is dose related, so reducing the corticosteroid to the lowest dose that controls the lung disease is the definitive step and must be negotiated with the treating team rather than decided unilaterally. An antipsychotic provides symptom control in the interim, and olanzapine has the best evidence in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose unchanged and review him again in one week
options.rationale: He is making financial commitments he cannot meet and has had four nights of severe sleep disruption, which represents active risk rather than a syndrome that can be observed. Waiting a week allows further irreversible decisions. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is strongly dose dependent, with risk rising sharply above the equivalent of about 40 mg of prednisolone daily and reaching close to one in five patients at doses above 80 mg. Onset is usually within the first two weeks of starting or increasing the dose. The presentation is more often elevated or mixed than depressive in the acute phase, while depressive syndromes are more characteristic of long term therapy and of the withdrawal period, and a hypoactive delirium can also occur, particularly in older patients. Importantly, a personal or family history of psychiatric illness is not a reliable predictor, so the absence of one offers no reassurance, whereas a previous episode on corticosteroid strongly predicts recurrence. Management prioritises reducing the dose to the minimum required for the underlying disease, which usually resolves the syndrome within days to weeks, with an antipsychotic used for symptom control in the interim and abrupt cessation avoided because of adrenal suppression.
key_points: Risk rises steeply above about 40 mg prednisolone equivalent daily
Onset is typically within the first two weeks of starting or increasing the dose
Elevated and mixed states predominate acutely, depression with chronic use and withdrawal
A negative psychiatric history does not predict who will be affected
Reduce the dose in negotiation with the treating team and never stop abruptly
explanation.pearls: A previous corticosteroid induced psychiatric episode is the single strongest predictor of another, so document it prominently and consider prophylactic olanzapine or lithium cover if a future high dose course above 40 mg prednisolone equivalent becomes necessary.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: distinguishing refreshing hypersomnolence with muscle tone loss from depressive hypersomnia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 22 year old university student referred with treatment resistant depression. He has had eighteen months of overwhelming daytime sleepiness, falling asleep in lectures, on the bus and once in the middle of a conversation with a friend.

He has completed adequate trials of two different antidepressants at therapeutic doses, and says that his mood lifted a little on the second but that the sleepiness was entirely unchanged. He sleeps eight to nine hours at night, wakes feeling refreshed, and says a fifteen minute nap leaves him clear headed for a couple of hours. He still enjoys music and seeing friends when he is awake enough. When you ask about his laughter, he describes his knees buckling and his jaw going slack for a few seconds when something strikes him as very funny.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, no retrognathia, Mallampati class 1, mental state examination shows mildly low but reactive mood with preserved interest and no anhedonia, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24, thyroid function within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, no snoring or witnessed apnoeas reported by his housemate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry and review the tracing in the clinic
options.rationale: Oximetry screens for obstructive sleep apnoea, the other major cause of excessive daytime sleepiness, and would be sensible if his history suggested it. He has a normal body mass index, no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and describes naps as refreshing, whereas sleepiness from apnoea is characteristically unrefreshed. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Trial of a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
options.rationale: Two adequate trials have already left the sleepiness untouched, and the features that would support a depressive hypersomnia are absent since he retains interest and wakes refreshed. A third trial repeats a strategy that has already failed for the dominant symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Measure thyroid function with iron studies and vitamin B12 levels
options.rationale: Screening for metabolic and haematological causes of fatigue is a reasonable general step and thyroid function and ferritin have already returned within normal limits. None of these tests explains the episodes of emotionally triggered weakness, which is the discriminating feature. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast within a month
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when a secondary cause is suspected, such as a hypothalamic or pineal region lesion, signalled by focal neurological signs, headache, visual change or endocrine disturbance. He has none of these and the yield in a typical presentation is very low. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, together with refreshing naps and preserved interest, points to a primary disorder of sleep and wake regulation rather than to depression. Overnight study followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test is the diagnostic standard, demonstrating a short mean sleep latency with early entry into rapid eye movement sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 arises from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, most likely through an autoimmune mechanism, and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, yet diagnostic delay commonly exceeds a decade and misdiagnosis as depression is among the commonest reasons, because both present with a young person who is sleepy, withdrawn and underperforming. Cataplexy is the near specific feature and consists of brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved, and it must be asked about directly because patients rarely volunteer it and often describe it only as weakness or as knees giving way. The remaining features are sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep. The discriminator against depressive hypersomnia is the quality of sleep and naps: in narcolepsy naps are brief and genuinely restorative and night sleep is not extended, whereas depressive hypersomnia produces long unrefreshing sleep, difficulty getting out of bed and naps that leave the person no better. Diagnosis rests on overnight polysomnography excluding other causes followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief emotion triggered bilateral tone loss with preserved consciousness
Patients rarely volunteer cataplexy, so ask directly about weakness when laughing
Refreshing brief naps distinguish narcolepsy from depressive hypersomnia
Antidepressant trials leave the sleepiness unchanged
Polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test is the diagnostic standard
explanation.pearls: Ask every sleepy young patient what happens to their body when they laugh hard: a description of jaw slackening, head nodding or knees buckling for a few seconds with full awareness is cataplexy and shifts the diagnosis from depression to narcolepsy in a single question.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists
